Check whether the priors of a fitted model pull its estimates

Source: R/check-prior.R
check_prior.Rd

Measures how much each estimate of a model fitted with fit_hazard() depends on its priors, block by block, by power-scaling (Kallioinen et al. 2024): each block of priors is raised to a power slightly above and below 1, the posterior is reweighted to match, and the change in each estimate's distribution is measured. An estimate that moves when one block is scaled is pulled by that block. A narrow prior can pull an estimate with no sign in the convergence diagnostics. That is most likely in a design whose groups fail far from the reference temperature or far from each other. log a is the log failure rate at the reference temperature, so a group that fails some degrees away has its log a extrapolated from its failures over that distance, a change of about b times the distance. A prior narrow beside that change draws log a back towards the prior's centre, and the group's other parameters move to fit its failures.

Usage

check_prior(fit, newdata = NULL, t_ref = NULL, p = 0.5, levels = NULL)

Arguments

fit

A brmsfit, a model fitted with fit_hazard().

newdata

A data frame of covariate values, one row per setting at which to check the reported parameters (and sCTmax, with t_ref), e.g. one row per species. It must hold every covariate in the model's parameter formulas, as in derive_tdt_ttl(), and the quantities are computed with the random effects at zero, as there. NULL (the default) checks the coefficients only.

t_ref

A single positive number, the reference exposure time for sCTmax, in the time unit of the data the model was fitted to. NULL (the default) leaves sCTmax out; it needs newdata.

p

A single number strictly between 0 and 1, the fraction failing within t_ref that defines sCTmax.

levels

A named numeric vector giving the level of each co-stressor, on its measurement scale, at which the parameters and sCTmax are checked; required with newdata when the model has co-stressors, as in derive_tdt_ttl(), and ignored, with a warning, without newdata.

Value

A list of two tibbles:

  • sensitivity, one row per block and quantity: block; quantity, a coefficient as brms names its draws (b_loga_Intercept) or, for each row of newdata, a reported parameter (a, b, shape, ...) or sCTmax; the columns of newdata, NA for a coefficient; prior and likelihood, the sensitivity to scaling the block and to scaling the likelihood; diagnosis, priorsense's reading of the two, in its own words; and k_prior and k_likelihood, the Pareto k of the scaling of the block and of the likelihood (see Reading the sensitivity).

  • priors, one row per population-level coefficient: parameter, coefficient, prior; prior_centre and prior_scale (the mean and standard deviation of a normal, the location and scale of a Student-t, NA for a flat prior); the posterior median and sd; distance, the median's distance from the prior's centre in units of its scale; and sd_ratio, the posterior standard deviation over the prior's scale.

Details

The model is not refitted. The check needs the log prior of each draw, which brms keeps, and the log-likelihood of each draw, which it computes once over all draws (about half a minute for 4000 draws of a model fitted to 14,000 rows).

Blocks of priors

The priors are scaled in blocks: one per parameter of the model (loga, logb, Tc, the baseline's parameters), holding its intercept and its slopes; one per co-stressor, named c<name> after its main effect, holding the main effect and the interaction with temperature; sd, holding every prior on a group-level term (standard deviations and correlations); and all, every prior together. The priors of the population-level coefficients are read from the fit and evaluated at each draw, and sd is the rest of the log prior brms kept. Without group-level terms that rest must be zero, which checks that the priors were read as brms used them. Normal and Student-t priors (and flat ones) on the coefficients can be read; any other is refused, as are bounds on the coefficients and terms other than linear and group-level ones (splines, monotonic effects). A block whose priors are all flat has nothing to scale and is left out, with a message.

Reading the sensitivity

priorsense reads the two sensitivities together, against a threshold of 0.05. When both are at or above it, the prior and the data disagree, and it reports a "potential prior-likelihood conflict". When only the sensitivity to the prior is above it, the prior rather than the data sets the estimate, and it reports a "potential strong prior / weak likelihood"; every other row reads "-". In a model with group-level terms, scaling the likelihood is like changing the number of individuals within each group, not the number of groups, so a quantity that the groups inform, such as their standard deviation, can show little likelihood sensitivity without the likelihood being weak (Kallioinen et al. 2024, section 2.5). The threshold marks a sensitivity that can be detected, not one that matters. In simulations of a design with three species whose failures lay some degrees apart, a sensitivity of the Weibull shape of 0.18 to 0.28 to the block loga came with a bias in the shape of about two and a half posterior standard deviations, while sensitivities up to 0.09 came with biases under a third of one; no fit fell between 0.09 and 0.18. Nor is the size of a sensitivity the size of a bias: in the same simulations sCTmax reached sensitivities of 0.06 to 0.12 while its bias was at most 0.08 degrees. The other blocks never exceeded 0.03.

Each scaling is an importance-sampling estimate, and the Pareto k of its weights says whether they can be trusted: k_prior is the larger k of the two scalings of the block and k_likelihood that of the likelihood's two. A k above priorsense's threshold (min(1 - 1 / log10(S), 0.7) for S draws; 0.7 from 4,000 draws) warns, and the sensitivities of that scaling are a sign at most. A block whose prior lies far from the posterior is where the weights degrade, and that is the case the check is for, so the warning is to be read rather than silenced.

The test of a flagged block is a refit with that block's priors widened (through intercept_priors and slope_prior of build_hazard_prior()), compared with the first fit. The table priors shows which coefficients lie far out in their prior or have a posterior almost as wide as it.

References

Kallioinen, N., Paananen, T., Burkner, P.-C. and Vehtari, A. (2024). Detecting and diagnosing prior and likelihood sensitivity with power-scaling. Statistics and Computing 34, 57.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# a model fitted to a small ramping trial: 20 individuals warmed from 20 to 35
# degrees over 60 minutes and checked every minute, in two trials (see fit_hazard())
path   <- data.frame(path_id = "A", time = c(0, 60), temp = c(20, 35))
checks <- data.frame(path_id = "A", time = seq(0, 60, by = 1))
ind    <- data.frame(id = 1:20, path_id = "A", event = 1, mass = runif(20, 8, 12),
                     trial = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 10),
                     t_upper = sample(seq(10, 60, 10), 20, replace = TRUE))
long   <- build_hazard_data(ind, path, "interval", covariates = c("mass", "trial"),
                            checks = checks)
fit    <- fit_hazard(long, "exp", dpar_formulas = list(loga = ~ 1 + mass))

chk <- check_prior(fit, newdata = data.frame(mass = c(8, 12)), t_ref = 60)
chk$sensitivity
chk$priors
} # }
